key: A. One fasting result at or above 92 mg/dL makes the diagnosis on this test
explanation summary: On the one-step 75-g test at 24 to 28 weeks, the diagnosis is made when any one value meets or exceeds fasting 92 mg/dL, 1-hour 180 mg/dL, or 2-hour 153 mg/dL. Fasting glucose is 97 mg/dL. The other two results are below their cutoffs, and a single abnormal result is enough.

key: B. The 1-hour result alone meets the one-step diagnostic threshold
explanation summary: The one-step criteria are fasting 92 mg/dL, 1-hour 180 mg/dL, and 2-hour 153 mg/dL, and any one value at or above its cutoff makes the diagnosis. The 1-hour value is 186 mg/dL. Fasting and 2-hour values are below their cutoffs.

key: C. The 2-hour result at or above 153 mg/dL establishes the diagnosis
explanation summary: On the one-step 75-g test, a 2-hour plasma glucose at or above 153 mg/dL is diagnostic even when the fasting and 1-hour values are below 92 and 180 mg/dL. This 2-hour result is 159 mg/dL.

key: D. None of the three results meets a one-step diagnostic cutoff
explanation summary: The one-step cutoffs are fasting 92 mg/dL, 1-hour 180 mg/dL, and 2-hour 153 mg/dL. All three results are below those cutoffs, so the test does not make the diagnosis.

key: E. Each result is just below its cutoff, so the test is not diagnostic
explanation summary: The diagnosis requires a value at or above fasting 92 mg/dL, 1-hour 180 mg/dL, or 2-hour 153 mg/dL. Results of 91, 179, and 152 mg/dL are each 1 mg/dL below the corresponding cutoff.

key: A. Repeat a 75-g test after an overnight fast of at least 8 hours
explanation summary: The one-step 75-g test is performed in the morning after an overnight fast of at least 8 hours. A test done 3 hours after breakfast does not meet that condition, so it should be repeated after a proper fast.

key: B. The 24-to-28-week one-step cutoffs should not be used to label this early test
explanation summary: ADA states that the IADPSG 75-g diagnostic criteria and the two-step criteria were not derived from data in the first half of pregnancy and should not be used for early screening. Before 15 weeks, testing looks for abnormal glucose metabolism and undiagnosed diabetes, not these later cutoffs.

key: C. Perform the routine glucose test at 24 to 28 weeks
explanation summary: If early testing has not shown diabetes or high-risk abnormal glucose metabolism, ADA recommends screening at 24 to 28 weeks. A normal early fasting glucose and A1C do not replace that screen.

key: D. One high fasting value does not meet the two-value rule
explanation summary: On the 100-g test, Carpenter-Coustan diagnosis needs at least two of fasting 95 mg/dL, 1-hour 180 mg/dL, 2-hour 155 mg/dL, and 3-hour 140 mg/dL. Fasting glucose is 101 mg/dL. The other three results are below their cutoffs, so only one value qualifies.

key: E. Only the 3-hour result is high, so two values are not met
explanation summary: Carpenter-Coustan rules on the 100-g test require at least two values at or above fasting 95, 1-hour 180, 2-hour 155, and 3-hour 140 mg/dL. Only the 3-hour result, 152 mg/dL, clears its cutoff.

key: A. The fasting and 2-hour results together meet the two-value rule
explanation summary: At least two Carpenter-Coustan values are required: fasting 95, 1-hour 180, 2-hour 155, and 3-hour 140 mg/dL. Fasting glucose is 99 mg/dL and the 2-hour glucose is 160 mg/dL, so two cutoffs are met.

key: B. The 1-hour and 3-hour results are a sufficient pair
explanation summary: Carpenter-Coustan criteria need at least two of fasting 95, 1-hour 180, 2-hour 155, and 3-hour 140 mg/dL. The 1-hour result is 191 mg/dL and the 3-hour result is 144 mg/dL.

key: C. Each 100-g result is below its cutoff, so the test is not positive
explanation summary: Carpenter-Coustan cutoffs are fasting 95, 1-hour 180, 2-hour 155, and 3-hour 140 mg/dL, and at least two are required. Results of 94, 179, 154, and 139 mg/dL are each below the matching cutoff.

key: D. Do not go on to a 100-g test at this practice's 140 mg/dL threshold
explanation summary: In the two-step approach, a 50-g screen is followed by a 100-g test when the 1-hour value meets the threshold that practice chose: 130, 135, or 140 mg/dL. This practice chose 140 mg/dL. The result is 133 mg/dL, which is below that threshold.

key: E. Proceed to the 100-g test because 130 mg/dL meets the chosen threshold
explanation summary: The 50-g screen leads to a 100-g test when the 1-hour glucose meets the threshold that practice chose, which may be 130, 135, or 140 mg/dL. This office uses 130 mg/dL, and the result is 130 mg/dL.

key: A. These 100-g cutoffs should not be used before 15 weeks
explanation summary: The 100-g and 75-g pregnancy criteria were not derived for the first half of pregnancy and should not be used before 15 weeks. This fasting value is under 126 mg/dL, so early testing has not shown diabetes. Screening still belongs at 24 to 28 weeks.

key: B. This fasting result meets the 126 mg/dL line and still needs confirmation
explanation summary: Nonpregnant criteria use fasting plasma glucose of 126 mg/dL or higher after at least 8 hours. This result is 136 mg/dL after 9 hours. Without unequivocal hyperglycemia, a second abnormal result is required before the diagnosis is final.

key: C. Diabetes was not shown, so screen at 24 to 28 weeks
explanation summary: Fasting plasma glucose of 116 mg/dL is under the diabetes threshold of 126 mg/dL, so this early test did not show diabetes. Pregnancy diagnostic cutoffs are not used before 15 weeks. Screening is performed at 24 to 28 weeks.

key: D. An A1C under 6.5% if that can be reached safely
explanation summary: Before conception, the A1C goal is under 6.5% when it can be reached safely. This result is 7.4%, and recent glucose readings have not shown hypoglycemia.

key: E. The pregnancy fasting goal is under 95 mg/dL, so 104 is above it
explanation summary: During pregnancy the fasting glucose goal is under 95 mg/dL. This fasting result is 104 mg/dL.

key: A. This fasting result meets the pregnancy goal of under 95 mg/dL
explanation summary: In pregnancy the fasting glucose goal is under 95 mg/dL. This fasting result is 88 mg/dL.

key: B. The 1-hour goal in pregnancy is under 140 mg/dL, so 156 is above it
explanation summary: In pregnancy the 1-hour postprandial goal is under 140 mg/dL. This 1-hour result is 156 mg/dL.

key: C. This 1-hour result meets the goal of under 140 mg/dL
explanation summary: The 1-hour postprandial goal in pregnancy is under 140 mg/dL. This result is 126 mg/dL.

key: D. The 2-hour goal is under 120 mg/dL, so 129 mg/dL is above it
explanation summary: In pregnancy the 2-hour postprandial goal is under 120 mg/dL. This 2-hour result is 129 mg/dL.

key: E. The pregnancy A1C goal is under 6% if hypoglycemia is absent
explanation summary: During pregnancy the A1C goal is under 6% if it can be reached without significant hypoglycemia. This A1C is 6.4%, and the lowest recent home glucose is 78 mg/dL.

key: A. Significant hypoglycemia allows the A1C goal to relax to under 7%
explanation summary: If the under-6% goal cannot be reached without significant hypoglycemia, the pregnancy A1C goal is relaxed to under 7%. Glucose values of 48, 51, and 46 mg/dL were accompanied by symptoms that resolved with glucose. The A1C is 6.7%.

key: B. Do not use the glucose management indicator during pregnancy
explanation summary: Glucose-management-indicator and estimated A1C calculations are not used in pregnancy. Fasting glucose this morning is 108 mg/dL, which is above the fasting goal of under 95 mg/dL.

key: C. Begin medical nutrition therapy, activity, and weight management
explanation summary: After this diagnosis, the initial step is medical nutrition therapy together with physical activity and weight management. Insulin is reserved for when those measures are not enough. Fasting glucose was 100 mg/dL and the 2-hour value was 162 mg/dL.

key: D. Raise carbohydrate intake to at least 175 g per day
explanation summary: The minimum carbohydrate intake in pregnancy is 175 g per day. A log of 96 g per day is below that floor and should be raised, even though the fasting glucose of 90 mg/dL is under the 95 mg/dL goal.

key: E. 168 g per day is still short of the 175 g daily minimum
explanation summary: Minimum carbohydrate intake in pregnancy is 175 g per day. A tally of 168 g per day is still short of that minimum. Fasting glucose is 94 mg/dL, under the 95 mg/dL goal, and the 1-hour value of 132 mg/dL is under the 140 mg/dL goal.

key: A. 175 g per day meets the pregnancy carbohydrate minimum
explanation summary: The minimum carbohydrate intake in pregnancy is 175 g per day. This printout is 175 g per day, so the minimum is met. Fasting glucose is 89 mg/dL, which is under the 95 mg/dL goal.

key: B. 236 g per day already satisfies the 175 g minimum
explanation summary: Minimum carbohydrate intake in pregnancy is 175 g per day. An intake of 236 g per day meets that minimum. Fasting glucose is 92 mg/dL, under the goal of 95 mg/dL.

key: C. Do not drop carbohydrate below 175 g per day to chase the glucose
explanation summary: Minimum carbohydrate intake in pregnancy is 175 g per day. A drop from about 180 g to 90 g would break that floor. The fasting glucose is 102 mg/dL, above the goal of under 95 mg/dL, and carbohydrate is not replaced with fat to chase it.

key: D. Do not replace carbohydrate with fat; restore intake to at least 175 g
explanation summary: Carbohydrate should not be replaced with fat to chase glucose. The pregnancy minimum is 175 g of carbohydrate per day, and this tally is 70 g. Fasting glucose is 101 mg/dL, above the goal of under 95 mg/dL.

key: E. The 175 g minimum still applies while this fasting result is at goal
explanation summary: Minimum carbohydrate intake in pregnancy is 175 g per day. An intake near 80 g is below that floor. The fasting glucose of 86 mg/dL does meet the goal of under 95 mg/dL, and that success does not erase the food minimum.

key: A. Adjust treatment without taking carbohydrate under 175 g per day
explanation summary: The 1-hour postprandial goal is under 140 mg/dL, and this result is 158 mg/dL, so the plan needs attention. Minimum carbohydrate intake stays 175 g per day. Insulin is first-line when lifestyle measures are not enough, and carbohydrate is not traded for fat.

key: B. Medical nutrition therapy, which walking does not replace
explanation summary: Initial care is medical nutrition therapy, activity, and weight management. She is already active on the scaffold. The missing piece is medical nutrition therapy. On the 100-g test, fasting 98 mg/dL and the 2-hour value of 159 mg/dL are two results at or above 95 and 155 mg/dL.

key: C. Keep medical nutrition therapy and include weight management
explanation summary: After the glucose diagnosis, care includes medical nutrition therapy, activity, and weight management. The meal plan of 190 g meets the 175 g carbohydrate minimum, and walking is already happening. Weight management still belongs in the plan. Fasting glucose is 90 mg/dL, under the goal of 95 mg/dL, and the 1-hour value is 128 mg/dL, under 140 mg/dL.

key: D. Start insulin; lifestyle has not met the fasting goal
explanation summary: When lifestyle measures are not enough, insulin is first-line. The carbohydrate intake is 188 g per day, above the 175 g minimum, and fasting values of 109, 112, and 107 mg/dL are above the goal of under 95 mg/dL. Metformin and glyburide cross the placenta and are not first-line.

key: E. Schedule the 75-g test between 4 and 12 weeks after birth
explanation summary: The postpartum test is a 75-g tolerance test at 4 to 12 weeks, read with nonpregnant criteria. Sixteen days is before that window, so today is too early.

key: A. Perform a 75-g tolerance test and use nonpregnant cutoffs
explanation summary: At 4 to 12 weeks postpartum the test is a 75-g oral tolerance test interpreted with nonpregnant criteria. Nine weeks is inside that window.

key: B. The A1C cannot clear her; a 75-g test is the postpartum study
explanation summary: The postpartum test, done at 4 to 12 weeks, is a 75-g tolerance test using nonpregnant criteria. A1C is lowered by increased red-cell turnover and by delivery blood loss, so this 5.8% result is not the deciding test. Seven weeks is inside the 4-to-12-week window, and hemoglobin is 8.9 g/dL after a 1400 mL loss.

key: C. The 2-hour value meets the 200 mg/dL line and needs confirmation
explanation summary: Nonpregnant criteria, which this 4-to-12-week 75-g test uses, call a 2-hour glucose at or above 200 mg/dL abnormal. This result is 214 mg/dL. She has no classic symptoms and is not in crisis, so a second abnormal result is required before the diagnosis is final. The fasting value of 93 mg/dL is under 100 mg/dL.

key: D. 181 mg/dL sits in the 140 to 199 mg/dL range, not at or above 200
explanation summary: On a 75-g test read with nonpregnant criteria, a 2-hour glucose of 140 to 199 mg/dL is the prediabetes range, and 200 mg/dL or higher is the diabetes-range line. This 2-hour result is 181 mg/dL. The fasting result of 90 mg/dL is under 100 mg/dL.

key: E. Rescreen every 1 to 3 years after this normal 75-g test
explanation summary: Nonpregnant criteria put a normal fasting glucose under 100 mg/dL and a normal 2-hour glucose under 140 mg/dL. These results are 84 and 118 mg/dL. After a normal postpartum test, rescreen every 1 to 3 years.

key: A. Start low-dose aspirin now, inside the 12-to-16-week window
explanation summary: People with preexisting type 1 or type 2 diabetes are offered low-dose aspirin, 100 to 150 mg per day, starting at 12 to 16 weeks. Daily insulin since age 13, before this pregnancy, is that preexisting pattern, and 14 weeks is inside the window. A dose of 162 mg per day may be acceptable.

key: B. Plan the start for 12 to 16 weeks, not for this visit
explanation summary: Low-dose aspirin, 100 to 150 mg per day, is started at 12 to 16 weeks for people with preexisting type 1 or type 2 diabetes. Metformin plus insulin for 11 years before conception fits that preexisting pattern. At 9 weeks the start is planned, not given today. A dose of 162 mg per day may be acceptable.

key: C. 100 to 150 mg daily, and 162 mg daily may be acceptable
explanation summary: For preexisting type 1 or type 2 diabetes, low-dose aspirin is 100 to 150 mg per day, started at 12 to 16 weeks. A dose of 162 mg per day may be acceptable, and US tablets are 81 mg. Insulin since a childhood ketoacidosis episode, still in use at 13 weeks, is the preexisting pattern.

key: D. Start or titrate treatment at the pregnancy threshold of 140/90 mm Hg
explanation summary: In pregnant people with diabetes and chronic hypertension, treatment is started or titrated at 140/90 mm Hg, not at the nonpregnant goal of 130/80. This reading is 146/94 mm Hg. A suggested goal is 110-135/85 mm Hg, and treatment is deintensified if the reading is under 90/60.

key: E. Do not intensify; the pregnancy threshold is 140/90, not 130/80
explanation summary: Treatment in pregnant people with diabetes and chronic hypertension is started or titrated at 140/90 mm Hg, not at 130/80. This reading is 134/82, which is below 140/90. It also sits in the suggested range of 110-135/85 mm Hg. Deintensifying is for readings under 90/60.

key: A. Deintensify treatment because the reading is under 90/60 mm Hg
explanation summary: In pregnant people with diabetes and chronic hypertension, deintensify treatment if blood pressure is under 90/60 mm Hg. This reading is 86/54. The start-or-titrate threshold is 140/90, and a suggested goal is 110-135/85. ACE inhibitors are not added in pregnancy.

key: B. Stop the ACE inhibitor before a planned conception
explanation summary: ACE inhibitors are stopped before conception. She is 36, the pregnancy test is negative, and conception is being planned. A separate preconception target is an A1C under 6.5% if safely achievable; her A1C is 6.8%, and that figure does not keep lisinopril in place. Angiotensin-receptor blockers and mineralocorticoid antagonists are stopped too, and statins are stopped in most cases.

key: C. Stop the angiotensin-receptor blocker before conception
explanation summary: Angiotensin-receptor blockers are stopped before conception. Losartan is in that class, and she is 30. ACE inhibitors and mineralocorticoid antagonists are stopped as well. Her A1C is 6.6%; the separate preconception A1C goal is under 6.5% if safely achievable, and that goal does not keep losartan going.

key: D. Stop the mineralocorticoid antagonist before conception
explanation summary: Mineralocorticoid antagonists are stopped before conception. Spironolactone is in that class. She is 34, and the drug is stopped even though the A1C is 6.4%, which is under the separate preconception goal of 6.5%. ACE inhibitors and angiotensin-receptor blockers are stopped as well.

key: E. Stop the statin before conception in most cases
explanation summary: In most cases, statins are stopped before conception. She is 41 and takes atorvastatin, and the pregnancy test is negative. The separate preconception A1C goal is under 6.5% if safely achievable; her A1C is 6.9%. Neither that gap nor the LDL cholesterol of 96 mg/dL is a reason to continue the statin into conception.

key: A. Stop it now; the first-trimester deadline has passed
explanation summary: Metformin used for polycystic ovary syndrome to induce ovulation should be stopped by the end of the first trimester. She is at 17 weeks, past that point, and the tablets are still in use. The fasting glucose is 84 mg/dL.

key: B. Use the plasma glucose; A1C is unreliable in this trimester
explanation summary: A1C is unreliable in the second and third trimesters and postpartum, so plasma glucose is used instead. This fasting plasma glucose is 112 mg/dL, above the pregnancy fasting goal of under 95 mg/dL. The A1C of 5.4% does not override that glucose.

key: C. Obtain a chlamydia NAAT at this first prenatal visit
explanation summary: Chlamydia screening in pregnancy is done at the first prenatal visit. A repeat in the third trimester is for age under 25 or increased risk, such as a new partner, more than one partner, or a partner with a sexually transmitted infection. She is 32, but this is the first visit, and no test has been done.

key: D. Repeat the chlamydia NAAT because she is younger than 25
explanation summary: A chlamydia test is done at the first prenatal visit and again in the third trimester when age is under 25, even without a new partner. She is 23, the early NAAT was negative, and she is at 30 weeks.

key: E. Repeat the chlamydia NAAT because of the new partner
explanation summary: Third-trimester chlamydia testing is repeated when age is under 25 or risk is increased. A new partner is an increased-risk reason. She is 38, with a negative NAAT at 11 weeks and a new partner for six weeks, at 31 weeks of gestation.

key: A. A third-trimester NAAT is not indicated by her age or these risks
explanation summary: Repeat testing in the third trimester is for age under 25 or increased risk, including a new partner, more than one partner, or a partner with a sexually transmitted infection. She is 35, the 12-week NAAT was negative, and none of those risk factors are described.

key: B. Azithromycin 1 g orally as a single dose
explanation summary: Pregnancy treatment is azithromycin 1 g orally once. The alternative is amoxicillin 500 mg orally three times daily for 7 days. Doxycycline is contraindicated in the second and third trimesters. The NAAT is positive for Chlamydia trachomatis at 20 weeks.

key: C. NAAT about 4 weeks after treatment, and again at 3 months
explanation summary: In pregnancy, the test of cure is a NAAT about 4 weeks after treatment, and retesting is also done at 3 months. She took azithromycin 1 g six days ago, so a sample today is too soon for the 4-week test.

key: D. One A1C at or above 6.5% still needs a second abnormal result
explanation summary: An A1C of 6.5% or higher is one abnormal result. Without unequivocal hyperglycemia, two abnormal results are required, either the same test twice or two different tests. He has no classic symptoms and is not in crisis, and this A1C is 6.8%.

key: E. The A1C and the fasting glucose are two different abnormal tests
explanation summary: Fasting plasma glucose of 126 mg/dL or higher and an A1C of 6.5% or higher are each abnormal. These results are 134 mg/dL after a 10-hour fast and an A1C of 6.6%. Two different tests are abnormal, which meets the requirement for confirmation when hyperglycemia is not unequivocal.

key: A. Random glucose at or above 200 mg/dL plus these symptoms is enough
explanation summary: A random plasma glucose of 200 mg/dL or higher plus classic symptoms, which include polyuria, polydipsia, and unexplained weight loss, is diagnostic. This glucose is 256 mg/dL, with large-volume urination, thirst, and a 6 kg loss. A second test is not required for unequivocal hyperglycemia.

key: B. A random value at or above 200 mg/dL without symptoms is not enough
explanation summary: Without classic symptoms or a crisis, a random glucose of 228 mg/dL is not the unequivocal finding that skips confirmation. Diagnosis uses the standard tests, and two abnormal results are required when hyperglycemia is not unequivocal.

key: C. A glucose at or above 200 mg/dL in a crisis needs no second test
explanation summary: A random glucose of 200 mg/dL or higher plus a crisis is diagnostic. This plasma glucose is 436 mg/dL in a hyperglycemic crisis, so a second confirming test is not required.

key: D. An A1C of 6.0% is inside the 5.7% to 6.4% range
explanation summary: An A1C of 5.7% to 6.4% is the prediabetes range. This result is 6.0%. It is not at or above the 6.5% diabetes line.

key: E. 111 mg/dL is inside the 100 to 125 mg/dL range
explanation summary: A fasting plasma glucose of 100 to 125 mg/dL is the prediabetes range, after at least 8 hours without caloric intake. This result is 111 mg/dL after 12 hours. The A1C of 5.5% is under 5.7%.

key: A. 164 mg/dL is inside the 140 to 199 mg/dL range
explanation summary: On a 75-g test, a 2-hour glucose of 140 to 199 mg/dL is the prediabetes range. This 2-hour result is 164 mg/dL. The fasting glucose of 92 mg/dL is under 100 mg/dL, and the A1C of 5.6% is under 5.7%.

key: B. Decline to sign from the sensor, and obtain a standard plasma test
explanation summary: Continuous glucose monitoring is not used to diagnose this condition. A standard plasma test, such as fasting glucose, a 75-g tolerance test, or an A1C when A1C is reliable, is required. The fingerstick of 174 mg/dL is under 200 mg/dL and is not a completed diagnostic study.

key: C. The A1C is unreliable; use the plasma glucose
explanation summary: A1C is unreliable in G6PD deficiency, so plasma glucose is used instead. This fasting plasma glucose is 139 mg/dL after 9 hours, which is at or above the 126 mg/dL line. Without unequivocal hyperglycemia, a second abnormal glucose result is still required.

key: D. Do not use the A1C; judge him with the plasma glucose
explanation summary: A1C is unreliable in people treated with hemodialysis, so plasma glucose is used. This fasting glucose is 152 mg/dL, at or above 126 mg/dL. Without unequivocal hyperglycemia, a second abnormal result is still required.

key: E. Recent transfusion makes this A1C unreliable
explanation summary: A1C is unreliable after recent transfusion, so plasma glucose is used. This fasting glucose is 144 mg/dL after 10 hours, at or above 126 mg/dL. A second abnormal result is still required because hyperglycemia is not unequivocal.

key: A. Hemolysis makes this hemoglobin A1C result unreliable
explanation summary: A1C is unreliable during hemolysis, so the plasma glucose is the test to use. Fasting glucose is 148 mg/dL after 8 hours, at or above 126 mg/dL. A confirming second result is still required without unequivocal hyperglycemia.

key: B. Erythropoietin therapy makes this A1C unreliable
explanation summary: A1C is unreliable during erythropoietin therapy, so plasma glucose is used. The 2-hour value on this 75-g test is 214 mg/dL, which is at or above 200 mg/dL. She has no classic symptoms and is not in crisis, so a second abnormal result is still required.

key: C. Metformin may continue, with higher risk in the 30 to 45 range
explanation summary: Metformin may be used when the eGFR is at least 30 mL/min/1.73 m2. Risk rises at 30 to 45, and it should not be used below 30. This eGFR is 36, so the drug may continue with that higher risk. The A1C is 7.6%.

key: D. Do not use metformin at an eGFR under 30
explanation summary: Metformin should not be used when the eGFR is under 30 mL/min/1.73 m2. This eGFR is 23. It may be used at or above 30, and risk rises between 30 and 45.

key: E. Check vitamin B12 while metformin continues
explanation summary: Metformin is associated with vitamin B12 deficiency, so B12 is checked periodically. He has taken it for five years without a level. The eGFR of 72 mL/min/1.73 m2 is above the range where use is restricted. Hemoglobin is 11.4 g/dL.

key: A. Add a GLP-1 receptor agonist or an SGLT2 inhibitor
explanation summary: With atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, include a GLP-1 receptor agonist and/or an SGLT2 inhibitor regardless of the A1C. The A1C is 6.7%, which is under the common nonpregnant goal of 7%, and the stent is the cardiovascular history. The benefit is not withheld because the A1C is already under 7%.

key: B. An SGLT2 inhibitor, for reduced or preserved ejection fraction
explanation summary: An SGLT2 inhibitor is recommended for heart failure, whether the ejection fraction is reduced or preserved, regardless of the A1C. The A1C is 6.8% and the ejection fraction is 58%, with heart failure documented. The eGFR of 64 does not bar the class.

key: C. An SGLT2 inhibitor or a GLP-1 receptor agonist with benefit
explanation summary: For CKD with an eGFR of 20 to 60 and/or albuminuria, use an SGLT2 inhibitor or a GLP-1 receptor agonist with demonstrated benefit, regardless of the A1C. The eGFR is 46 and albuminuria is documented. The A1C is 6.5%.

key: D. Glucose lowering from the SGLT2 inhibitor is reduced below an eGFR of 45
explanation summary: The glycemic effect of SGLT2 inhibitors falls when the eGFR is under 45. This eGFR is 40, and the A1C is 8.4%. When the eGFR is under 30, a GLP-1 receptor agonist is preferred for glucose lowering. That second line is not yet the situation at 40.

key: E. A GLP-1 receptor agonist, preferred at this eGFR
explanation summary: When the eGFR is under 30, a GLP-1 receptor agonist is preferred for glucose lowering. The eGFR is 27, the A1C is 8.8%, and the fasting glucose is 188 mg/dL. There is no weight loss or ketosis, the glucose is under 300 mg/dL, and the A1C is not above 10%, so insulin is not required by those triggers. The glycemic effect of an SGLT2 inhibitor is already reduced under an eGFR of 45.

key: A. Do not combine the DPP-4 inhibitor with a GLP-1 receptor agonist
explanation summary: A DPP-4 inhibitor should not be combined with a GLP-1 receptor agonist. She is taking sitagliptin, a DPP-4 inhibitor, and the A1C is 8.2%. The fasting glucose is 154 mg/dL, under 300 mg/dL, and there are no catabolic features.

key: B. A GLP-1 receptor agonist in preference to insulin
explanation summary: If there is no insulin deficiency, a GLP-1 receptor agonist is preferred to insulin. The A1C is 8.3%, the glucose is 176 mg/dL, weight is stable, and ketones are negative. Those findings do not meet the insulin triggers of glucose at or above 300 mg/dL, A1C above 10%, or catabolic features.

key: C. Start insulin because the glucose is at or above 300 mg/dL
explanation summary: Start insulin when glucose is at least 300 mg/dL, when the A1C is above 10%, or when catabolic features such as weight loss and ketosis are present. This glucose is 328 mg/dL.

key: D. Start insulin because the A1C is above 10%
explanation summary: Insulin is started when the A1C is above 10%, even if other triggers are absent. This A1C is 10.8%. The random glucose is 214 mg/dL, which is under 300 mg/dL, and ketones are negative, but the A1C trigger is already met.

key: E. Start insulin now because of the weight loss and ketosis
explanation summary: Insulin is started when catabolic features are present, including weight loss and ketosis, as well as when glucose is at least 300 mg/dL or the A1C is above 10%. He has lost 8 kg and has urine ketones. The glucose is 246 mg/dL and the A1C is 9.2%, so those two numeric triggers are not the ones firing.

key: A. Do not add an SGLT2 inhibitor for glucose control
explanation summary: SGLT2 inhibitors increase DKA risk in type 1 diabetes and should not be added for glucose control. Insulin since age 8, after childhood ketoacidosis, is that setting. The A1C is 7.9% and the glucose is 186 mg/dL.

key: B. The A1C goal for many nonpregnant adults is under 7%
explanation summary: The A1C goal is under 7% for many nonpregnant adults without significant hypoglycemia. This A1C is 7.8%, and the lowest recent home glucose is 98 mg/dL.

key: C. 6.6% is already under the 7% goal
explanation summary: The A1C goal is under 7% for many nonpregnant adults without significant hypoglycemia. This result is 6.6%, and he has not had significant hypoglycemia.

key: D. A glucose of 63 mg/dL is level 1 hypoglycemia
explanation summary: Level 1 hypoglycemia is a glucose under 70 mg/dL and at or above 54 mg/dL. This reading is 63 mg/dL, and the repeat is 61 mg/dL. Level 2 is under 54 mg/dL.

key: E. A glucose of 49 mg/dL is level 2 hypoglycemia
explanation summary: Level 2 hypoglycemia is a glucose under 54 mg/dL. This reading is 49 mg/dL. Level 1 is under 70 and at or above 54 mg/dL.

key: A. A glucose of 54 mg/dL is level 1, not level 2
explanation summary: Level 1 hypoglycemia is a glucose under 70 mg/dL and at or above 54 mg/dL. Level 2 is under 54 mg/dL. This glucose is 54 mg/dL, so it is level 1.

key: B. Glucose tablets or other carbohydrate that contains glucose
explanation summary: For conscious hypoglycemia, give glucose or carbohydrate that contains glucose. This glucose is 58 mg/dL, which is level 1 because it is under 70 and at or above 54. Recheck in 15 minutes and repeat if it is still low. A high-fat or high-protein food is not the treatment.

key: C. Give oral glucose, because she is awake and can swallow
